title: Language Families and Relatedness
description: How to tell if languages share a common ancestor

concepts.title: What Is a Language Family?
concepts.contentHtml:
A language family is a group of languages descended from a common ancestor. The ancestor is called the proto-language. Languages in a family are cognate — related by descent, not by chance or borrowing.

The Indo-European family includes English, Spanish, Russian, Hindi, Persian, and Greek — all descended from Proto-Indo-European (PIE), spoken roughly 5,000–7,000 years ago. Evidence: systematic similarities in vocabulary and grammar that can't be explained by coincidence or borrowing.

Other major families: Sino-Tibetan (Mandarin, Tibetan), Afro-Asiatic (Arabic, Hebrew, Hausa), Niger-Congo (Swahili, Yoruba, Zulu), Austronesian (Malay, Hawaiian, Tagalog), Turkic (Turkish, Uzbek, Kazakh). About 400 language families are known.

concepts.title: Cognates vs Borrowings vs False Friends
concepts.contentHtml:
Cognates are words in different languages that descend from the same ancestral form. English father, German Vater, Latin pater, Sanskrit pitṛ — all from PIE *ph₂tḗr.

Borrowings (loanwords) are words taken from another language at a specific historical moment. English tsunami from Japanese, algebra from Arabic, tycoon from Japanese taikun. Borrowings are not evidence of common descent.

False friends are words that sound alike across languages but differ in meaning: Spanish embarazada means 'pregnant', not 'embarrassed'. Japanese mansion means a luxury apartment. False friends expose the traps of naive comparison.

concepts.title: The Comparative Method
concepts.contentHtml:
The comparative method is the systematic procedure for establishing language relationships and reconstructing proto-languages. Steps:

  1. Collect potential cognates from multiple languages (basic vocabulary: body parts, numbers, pronouns, which resist borrowing)
  2. Identify regular sound correspondences (not random similarities)
  3. Reconstruct the ancestral form that best explains the pattern

Example: Latin pater, Greek patḗr, Sanskrit pitṛ, English father all correspond in a regular pattern (p/p/p/f for the initial consonant — Grimm's Law accounts for the f). The proto-form *ph₂tḗr is reconstructed to explain all descendants. This method, developed in the 19th century, is the foundation of historical linguistics.

title: Sound Change and Grimm's Law
description: Regular, predictable shifts that link languages across millennia

concepts.title: Regular Sound Change — The Neogrammarian Hypothesis
concepts.contentHtml:
The 19th-century Neogrammarians (Brugmann, Osthoff) proposed that sound changes are exceptionless: when a sound changes, it does so in all words where it occurs, not selectively. This 'Neogrammarian hypothesis' was radical and controversial — it allowed historical linguistics to become scientific.

Evidence: Latin /p/ corresponds to Old English /f/ in pater/fæder, piscis/fisc (fish), pes/fōt (foot). Every Latin /p/ at the start of a word has a corresponding English /f/ — not just in some words. Apparent exceptions are explained by analogy, borrowing, or additional sound rules — not by random drift.

concepts.title: Grimm's Law
concepts.contentHtml:
Jacob Grimm (1822) described a systematic shift of stops in Proto-Germanic relative to PIE:

  • PIE voiceless stops *p, *t, *k → Germanic fricatives f, þ, h: PIE *pṓds → English foot (Latin pēs); PIE *tréyes → English three (Latin trēs); PIE *ḱerd- → English heart (Latin cor)
  • PIE voiced stops *b, *d, *g → Germanic voiceless stops p, t, k
  • PIE voiced aspirates *bh, *dh, *gh → Germanic voiced fricatives/stops

This is not cherry-picking — the shift applies to the entire stop series. Grimm's Law was later refined by Verner's Law (Karl Verner, 1875), which explained apparent exceptions by showing stress position conditioned the change.

concepts.title: Types of Sound Change
concepts.contentHtml:
Sound changes fall into categories based on mechanism:

  • Assimilation: a sound becomes more like a neighbor. Latin ad + ferō → afferō (d assimilates to f)
  • Dissimilation: a sound becomes less like a neighbor to avoid repetition. Latin peregrinus → Spanish peregrino → English pilgrim
  • Lenition (weakening): consonants weaken in intervocalic position. Latin vitam → Spanish vida (t → d)
  • Merger and split: two phonemes collapse into one (merger), or one splits into two in different environments

Sound changes are often motivated by articulation — assimilation makes adjacent sounds easier to produce; lenition reduces articulatory effort between vowels.

title: Proto-Indo-European and Language Reconstruction
description: Reconstructing a language spoken 6,000 years ago from its descendants

concepts.title: What We Know About PIE
concepts.contentHtml:
Proto-Indo-European (PIE) was spoken roughly 4500–3500 BCE, probably on the Pontic steppe (modern Ukraine/Russia). It has no direct written records — it is entirely reconstructed from its descendants.

William Jones (1786) famously noted the structural affinity between Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin, suggesting a common source. By the 19th century, systematic comparative work had reconstructed much of PIE's phonology, morphology, and some vocabulary.

PIE had a complex case system (eight cases), grammatical gender, and an ablaut (vowel alternation) system. Key reconstructed words: *ped- (foot), *mr̥tó- (dead), *wódr̥ (water). The asterisk (*) marks reconstructed, unattested forms.

concepts.title: The Indo-European Family Tree
concepts.contentHtml:
PIE split into major branches, each a family in its own right:

  • Indo-Iranian: Sanskrit, Hindi, Urdu, Persian, Bengali — largest by speakers
  • Germanic: English, German, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian
  • Romance: Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian
  • Balto-Slavic: Russian, Polish, Czech, Lithuanian, Latvian
  • Hellenic: Greek
  • Celtic: Welsh, Irish, Breton
  • Anatolian: Hittite (extinct, but the oldest attested IE branch)

The 'family tree' model is a simplification — contact and mixing between branches happen. A 'wave model' (Schmidt, 1872) complements the tree, showing features spreading across dialects like ripples.

concepts.title: Ablaut and PIE Morphology
concepts.contentHtml:
Ablaut (vowel gradation) is a systematic vowel alternation used to mark grammatical distinctions in PIE and its descendants. The alternation *e/*o/*zero is preserved in English:

  • sing / sang / sung (e-grade, o-grade, zero-grade)
  • drive / drove, ride / rode, write / wrote

In German: binden / band / gebunden (bind). These 'strong verb' patterns are fossil ablaut from PIE. Sanskrit shows the full system clearly, which is why Sanskrit was so important to early comparativists.

Ablaut persisted in Germanic because it was structurally integrated — it wasn't random vowel change but a functional grammatical marker. Recognizing ablaut patterns reveals the deep heritage English shares with Sanskrit and Greek.

title: Etymology and Semantic Change
description: How word meanings shift over centuries

concepts.title: Types of Semantic Change
concepts.contentHtml:
Word meanings are not fixed — they drift, expand, narrow, and invert over time:

  • Broadening (generalization): a word's meaning expands. Dog once referred to one specific breed; now it means any canine. Arrive originally meant to reach shore (from Latin ad ripam = to the bank).
  • Narrowing (specialization): Meat once meant food in general (Old English mete); now specifically animal flesh. Girl once meant any young person.
  • Amelioration: a word improves in meaning. Knight once meant 'boy/servant'; now denotes honor.
  • Pejoration: a word worsens. Villain meant 'farm worker'; silly meant 'blessed/happy' in Old English.

concepts.title: Etymology — Tracing Word Histories
concepts.contentHtml:
Etymology traces the history of individual words. It reveals how history, culture, and language change interact.

Examples: Salary from Latin salarium — possibly payment in salt, a precious Roman commodity. Disaster from Italian disastro (bad star — from astrology). Paradise from Old Iranian pairidaeza (walled garden).

False etymologies ('folk etymologies') are also revealing: Posh is popularly claimed to stand for 'Port Out, Starboard Home' (colonial ship cabin bookings) — but there's no historical evidence. People construct satisfying stories for word origins. Etymology requires documentary evidence, not plausible narratives.

concepts.title: Language Contact and Borrowing
concepts.contentHtml:
Languages in contact borrow vocabulary, sounds, and structures. English is an extreme case: roughly 60% of its vocabulary is borrowed from French (via the Norman Conquest, 1066) and Latin/Greek, with a Germanic core.

The result: English has doublets — pairs of words for the same concept with different registers. Germanic: begin, ask, house, eat. French: commence, enquire, mansion, dine. Latin/Greek: initiate, interrogate, domicile, consume.

Contact can produce creoles — when speakers of different languages form a stable mixed language. Haitian Creole draws vocabulary from French but grammar that substantially departed from it. The study of contact languages reveals what elements of language are most transferable — and what the 'substrate' languages contribute.

title: Language Death, Revival, and Deep Time
description: Endangered languages, the limits of reconstruction, and the Nostratic question

concepts.title: Language Death and Endangerment
concepts.contentHtml:
Of the estimated 7,000 languages spoken today, more than half are endangered — with fewer than 1,000 speakers, often elderly. At current rates, 50–90% may disappear by the end of this century.

Language death typically follows a pattern: younger generations switch to a dominant language (for economic or social reasons), a generation of semi-speakers emerges, and finally the last fluent speakers die. Language shift is usually voluntary but economically coerced.

Each language death is an irreversible loss: a unique way of encoding experience, ecological knowledge, and cultural memory. Languages like Ubykh (Northwest Caucasian, extinct 1992) had 84 consonants — a phonological system unlike any living language. Documenting endangered languages before they vanish is an urgent task in linguistics.

concepts.title: Language Revival — Hebrew as a Case Study
concepts.contentHtml:
Hebrew is the most successful case of language revival in history. After the second century CE, Hebrew was no longer spoken as a daily language (it continued as a liturgical and literary language). In the late 19th century, Eliezer Ben-Yehuda spearheaded its revival as a spoken vernacular in Palestine.

Modern Hebrew (Ivrit) drew on Biblical Hebrew grammar but adapted extensively: new vocabulary was coined for modern concepts (newspaper = iton from 'time'), foreign words were adapted, and phonology shifted. Today Hebrew is the first language of ~5 million people.

Welsh revival (Cymraeg) is another ongoing case: Welsh declined through the 20th century but has stabilized and grown through education policy, broadcasting (S4C), and active community use — now ~800,000 speakers. Language policy can genuinely reverse decline.

concepts.title: Deep Time and Proto-World
concepts.contentHtml:
The comparative method reliably reconstructs languages up to about 8,000–10,000 years back. Beyond this, regular sound correspondences are washed out by accumulated change and the signal-to-noise ratio collapses.

Some linguists have proposed macro-families linking established families. Nostratic (Dolgopolsky, Greenberg) proposes grouping Indo-European, Afro-Asiatic, Uralic, Altaic, Dravidian, and Kartvelian into a super-family. Joseph Greenberg proposed Amerind, grouping most Native American languages. These proposals remain highly controversial — most historical linguists regard them as undemonstrated.

The search for 'Proto-World' (a single ancestral human language) is romantic but probably unworkable with standard methods. Whether all human languages share a single origin is an open question — genetics and archaeology inform but cannot resolve it.
